newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - Payrolls on tap.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - Payrolls on tap.

text.p: U.S. debt markets should remain well bid on Friday unless the July employment data reveal the emergence of wage-driven inflationary pressures, analysts predicted.

"There is not going to be anything in particular to trouble the bond market. Therefore, I expect this grinding rally to continue," said John Ryding, senior economist at Bear Stearns and Co Inc, who expected more portfolio adjustments by mortgage-backed securities holders -- an important factor in the Treasury market's latest rally.

The recent decline in market rates is expected to generate further homeowners' refinancing which result in prepayments. This would force mortgage-backed holders to reinvest funds in Treasuries or other non-callable securities.
However, Treasuries are vulnerable to a short-term selloff if Friday's economic data point to exuberant economic growth.

The Labor Department is set to release the July payrolls at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT. Economists in a Reuters poll forecast 193,000 payroll jobs were created in July against 217,000 in June. They also expected the unemployment rate down 0.1 percent 4.9 percent.
Analysts said they will focus on the average hourly earnings component for hints of inflationary pressures.
The consensus among economists puts average hourly earnings up 0.2 percent in July versus June's up 0.3 percent.
Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy is calling for 148,000 new jobs, a three-cent increase in average hourly earnings, and an unemployment rate of 4.9 percent.
"It's a moderate report. It's consistent with what I think is going to be pretty solid growth and still relatively limited inflation in the third quarter," Liro said.
Market watchers agreed that any surprises in the employment report could easily trigger a swift market reaction in either direction.
But analysts said their long-term outlook on the U.S. economy is unlikely to change.
"If we were to see some strength in employment, you can get a reasonably significant one day consolidation," said Aubrey G. Lanston director of research Alan Levenson.
The credit market will also get the latest readings on personal income and spending data -- a sector much watched by the Fed.
On average, experts estimated that both personal income and consumption rose 0.4 percent in June versus a 0.3-percent rise in the prior month.

At 1000 EDT/1400 GMT, market players will have to contend with three more reports -- the June factory orders, the National Association of Purchasing Management's (NAPM) July survey and the University of Michigan's consumer sentiment index for July.

The market may watch for the NAPM's price component since a regional survey of Chicago manufacturers on Thursday showed some price pressures in July. The overall NAPM index is expected to be reported at 56.1 versus 55.7 in June.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was up 13/32 at 104-11/32 to yield 6.30 percent in late trading on Thursday. The federal funds rate is expected to open around 5.625 percent.
